newsitem.title: FRANCE: Suez sells property portfolio, predicts profit.
newsitem.headline: Suez sells property portfolio, predicts profit.

text.p: Venerable French holding company Cie de Suez said on Monday it would earn a profit in 1996, ending two years of huge losses due to bad property investments.

Suez chairman Gerard Mestrallet said the company would earn a 1996 consolidated profit of about 800 million francs ($145 million) after exceptional charges of three billion francs on property and other investments.

"I can confirm our return to profit in 1996," Mestrallet told reporters, adding that he expected a 25-percent rise in the group's 1996 pre-tax, pre-exceptional profit. He said he expected that result to climb again this year.

He also announced the sale of a property loan portfolio worth about four billion francs to real estate fund Whitehall Street Real Estate Limited Partnership VII, run by U.S. investment bank Goldman Sachs.

Mestrallet said the sale, for about three billion francs or 30 percent of the property's original value on the company's books, would result in a charge in 1996 of about one billion francs on the already heavily-provisioned portfolio.
Mestrallet was upbeat at a news conference called to announce the profit forecast, highlighting what he called a profound change in the company's strategy and financial situation during 1996.
The key events leading to that change were the sale of investment banking arm Banque Indosuez and the taking of a majority stake in Belgian utility Tractebel.

"We started the year as a banking group and we ended it as an industrial holding company," Mestrallet said. He added that the company had begun the year with five billion francs of debt and finished it with nearly five billion in cash.
"What is important in my view is that we have consolidated the group by drastically reducing, even completely eliminating, our biggest risks," he told reporters.

Though it cut its real estate exposure drastically in 1996, Suez still retains 4.9 billion francs of property loans it plans to sell, and another 3.1 billion francs in real estate that the company was spinning into a separate, fully-owned real estate holding company.

In the previous two years, Suez lost a total of 8.7 billion francs, mostly due to gargantuan provisions on its property business. Mestrallet said the company's adventure into real estate had cost it a calamitous 27.5 billion francs over the last four or five years.
Suez has pledged to exit the real estate business by 2001. ($1=5.523 French Franc)
